1310.title: Tara's mantra
1310.hook: om tare tuttare ture soha, the mantra of Tara
1310.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists recite Tara's mantra, om tare tuttare ture soha, often on a mala, in daily practice, in times of fear or danger, and on behalf of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deity yoga: seeing yourself as an awakened figure, empty and bright. Your line: as the deity.

Om tare tuttare ture soha. Said slowly, it has a shape: a long opening, three words that tumble down like steps, then a soft landing. Said fast, under the breath, it can sound like water running over stones. People in Tibetan Buddhist communities say it in kitchens and on buses, over sick children and before long journeys, often counting on a string of beads. You first met Tara back in year one, one foot already stepping down. Today, the sound that calls her.
screen: `A LONG OPENING, THREE STEPS, A LANDING.` → `IN KITCHENS AND ON BUSES.` → `THE SOUND THAT CALLS HER.`

segments.voice: First, who Tara is: a female bodhisattva, an awakened being who stays to help. One story says she was born from the tears of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, as he wept over the suffering of the world. Another tells of a princess who was told to pray to be reborn as a man, and instead vowed to wake up, and keep helping, as a woman. Second, the mantra. It's Sanskrit, and it plays on her own name, often explained as she who carries across, or she who saves. Tare, tuttare, ture: the name turned three ways, like calling someone, then calling again more urgently. Om opens it, and soha, the Tibetan way of saying the Sanskrit svaha, closes it, as it closes many mantras. Third, quickness. Tibetan devotion calls Tara swift. In her green form she's seated, left leg drawn in for meditation, right foot stepping down off her lotus. Teachers say that foot shows she's ready to rise the moment she's called. That's your line: she comes quickly. Fourth, how it's used. Some recite it in danger or fear, some for someone else's sake, some simply as a daily practice, letting the sound steady the mind. Tradition holds that the mantra is a way to meet her compassion.
screen: `A BODHISATTVA, BORN OF TEARS.` · `HER NAME, TURNED THREE WAYS.` · `ONE FOOT STEPPING DOWN.` · `IN FEAR, FOR OTHERS, EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `SHE COMES QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: If you wish, say it seven times, aloud or under your breath, slowly, counting on your fingers: om tare tuttare ture soha. If someone you know is frightened or struggling, you can hold them in mind while you chant; if chanting isn't yours, hear the rhythm in your head, or count seven slow breaths instead. Then rest in the quiet after the last soha.
Tara's mantra. Om tare tuttare ture soha: her name, called three ways, for the bodhisattva known as swift. Today's word.
Your line: she comes quickly. One foot already stepping down off the lotus. I'll be here tomorrow.

1311.title: The Medicine Buddha's mantra
1311.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists recite the Medicine Buddha's mantra for the sick, for the dying and for their own health, often with a visualization of the blue Medicine Buddha, and Medicine Buddha practices are held for people who are ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tara's mantra, her name called three ways. Your line: she comes quickly.

On the wall of a Tibetan clinic or a family shrine, there's sometimes a painting of a buddha who looks different from the others. His body is deep blue, the blue of lapis lazuli. In his left hand, resting in his lap, is a bowl. In his right, held out toward you, a branch with a small fruit. The bowl isn't for alms. He's holding medicine. Some people chant his mantra at hospital bedsides, and some keep it running quietly on their own bad days. You met him in his sutra on day eleven ninety-nine. Today, his mantra.
screen: `A BUDDHA THE COLOR OF LAPIS.` → `A BOWL, A BRANCH.` → `HE'S HOLDING MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: First, who he is. His Sanskrit name, Bhaishajyaguru, is usually translated medicine teacher. A sutra about him tells how, long ago, as a bodhisattva, he vowed that those who are sick, poor or without help would be relieved when they hear his name. Second, the mantra. In Sanskrit: tadyatha om bhaishajye bhaishajye mahabhaishajye raja samudgate svaha. In Tibetan it's often said: teyata om bekandze bekandze maha bekandze radza samungate soha. You can hear the word for medicine in it, called twice, then called great. Third, two kinds of sickness. The mantra is chanted for bodies: a fever, a diagnosis, a friend in surgery. Teachers also point to a deeper illness Buddhist teaching names, the three poisons of greed, hatred and delusion. The medicine in the bowl, they say, is for both. Tibetan medical tradition even presents its root medical text as taught by the Medicine Buddha. Fourth, alongside care, not instead of it. The same tradition that honors him built a whole system of medicine, with doctors and remedies. The chant belongs beside that care: it steadies the mind, gathers compassion and sends good wishes, while the body gets real treatment. And so it often turns outward. It's said for healing, wherever it's needed.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is unwell, in body or in spirit; if it's you, that's allowed. If you'd like, picture a deep blue light like the Medicine Buddha's resting over them, calm and steady, and silently, in your own plain words, wish that they heal, that their pain eases, that they're cared for. If you know the mantra and it's yours to say, you can say it softly.
The Medicine Buddha's mantra. A chant to the blue buddha of healing, said for bodies and for the deeper sickness of the mind. Today's word.
Your line: for healing. For bodies, and for the mind's deeper sickness too. See you tomorrow.

1312.title: Butter lamps
1312.hook: lamps of butter offered in temples as light
1312.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists light butter lamps on home shrines and in temples, often bringing butter as an offering, and light them on holy days, for the sick and for the dead; the flame is explained as wisdom dispelling darkness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medicine Buddha's mantra, said for bodies and minds. Your line: for healing.

The smell reaches you before the light does: warm, a little smoky, a little like a kitchen. Then the room opens up. Row after row of small metal bowls on long shelves, each holding a soft pool of melted butter and a single cotton wick, each burning. A woman in a long apron walks the rows with a pitcher, topping them up, the way someone waters plants. A pilgrim beside her tips a spoonful of butter from a jar she carried from home into one bowl, and moves on without a word. In Tibetan temples, light is something you give.
screen: `THE SMELL ARRIVES FIRST.` → `ROWS OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `A SPOONFUL FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. A butter lamp is a bowl of clarified butter with a wick, set before an image of the Buddha on a home shrine or in a temple hall. Tibetans call it chöme, an offering lamp. Families light them at home; pilgrims bring butter, or pay a little for a lamp to be lit, and temples keep many burning through the day. Light sits among the classic shrine offerings, with water, flowers, incense and food. Second, what the light means. Tibetan teachers explain the lamp as wisdom, the light that clears away the darkness of not seeing. Lighting one wishes that clarity for yourself and for others. People light them on holy days, for someone who is sick, and for someone who has died, the flame carrying a wish the way a letter carries words. Third, a story you met back in year one: the poor woman's lamp. She had almost nothing, begged a few coins, bought a little oil, and lit one small lamp among the grand lamps of kings. By morning the great lamps had burned out. Hers still burned, and when a disciple tried to put it out, it would not go out. In the story, the Buddha says it burns on because of the heart that lit it. Fourth, so the offering isn't measured by how much butter is in the bowl. A spoonful from a jar carried from home counts. The tradition cares about the intention: the wish that someone, somewhere, sees a little more clearly because of it.

segments.voice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it; if not, a small lamp or even a phone screen turned low will do. Watch the flame for a few breaths, and let it stand for a wish: that someone you know sees their way a little more clearly today. When you're done, blow it out gently.
Butter lamps. Small bowls of butter and a wick, lit before the Buddha in Tibetan homes and temples: light offered as a sign of wisdom clearing the dark. Today's word.
Your line: a lamp offered. A spoonful from home counts, lit with the whole heart. Go gently.

1313.title: Walking around
1313.hook: circling a temple, stupa or mountain clockwise, turning prayer wheels
1313.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists walk kora clockwise around temples, stupas, monasteries and sacred mountains, often reciting mantras, counting beads and turning prayer wheels as they go; some walk a short kora daily and others make long pilgrimages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, butter lamps, light given as a wish for clarity. Your line: a lamp offered.

Early morning, and the street around the temple is already moving, but nobody is walking straight anywhere. An old man in a sheepskin coat shuffles along, beads clicking through his fingers. Two teenagers pass him, talking about something on a phone. A woman spins a small handheld drum on a stick as she walks. Every one of them goes the same way, clockwise, around the same building, and when they reach where they started, some just keep going. It looks like a crowd that lost its map. It's a practice. Today's word: kora.
screen: `A STREET THAT ONLY GOES ONE WAY.` → `BEADS, PHONES, SPINNING DRUMS.` → `ROUND, AND ROUND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Kora is Tibetan for walking around something holy: a temple, a stupa, a monastery, a lake, a whole mountain. Tibetan Buddhists walk it clockwise, so the holy place stays on their right, the side of respect. Some walk it every day before work; some circle a whole mountain, a journey of days. Second, the roots, which are old, and which you met at the stupas in year three. In the Pali discourses, visitors who finish speaking with the Buddha sometimes rise, bow, and leave with the Buddha on their right. King Ajatasattu, who came to the Buddha by night, does exactly that before he goes. Third, the wheels. Along many kora routes stand prayer wheels, cylinders filled with rolled paper printed with mantras, often om mani padme hum. Walkers set them spinning clockwise as they pass, or carry small handheld wheels, like the woman in the street. Tibetan teachers say turning the wheel is like reciting the mantra inside it, and that it carries the wish for all beings to be free of suffering. Fourth, what the circle does. A straight road goes somewhere. A circle goes nowhere new, and that's the point. Each lap, the same doorways, the same stones, and the mind is asked again and again to come back to the center. Teachers say a kora can be walked with a mantra, with a prayer, or simply with attention to the feet.
screen: `KORA: WALKING AROUND THE HOLY.` · `KEEPING THE BUDDHA ON THE RIGHT.` · `WHEELS FULL OF MANTRAS.` · `A ROAD THAT GOES NOWHERE NEW.` · then, large: `WALK THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: If you can step outside, walk once around your block, your building or your yard, clockwise, keeping the center on your right; if not, walk slowly around a table or a chair. Feel each foot land, and keep one thing in mind as your center: a person you love, a wish, or simply the place itself. When you get back to where you started, pause and notice that you're home.
Kora. Tibetan for walking around a holy place, clockwise, keeping it on your right, often with beads, a mantra, or a turning prayer wheel. Today's word.
Your line: walk the circle. The circle holds whatever you bring. See you on the next lap.

1314.title: Mani stones
1314.hook: stones carved with mantras, piled along paths and passes
1314.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhist regions, stones carved with om mani padme hum and other mantras are left at passes, bridges, villages and stupas, where they build up into long mani walls; travelers pass them clockwise, keeping them on the right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kora, the walk around the holy. Your line: walk the circle.

A trail climbs toward a high pass. No trees, thin air, wind that doesn't stop. Beside the path runs a low wall that isn't really a wall: flat stones stacked together, more than anyone could count at a glance, some gray and plain, some painted blue, red, yellow and white. Look closer and every one is carved, the same six syllables over and over, cut into rock by hands you'll never meet. A walker steps to the left so the wall stays on her right, sets one more stone on the pile, and keeps climbing. Today: mani stones.
screen: `A WALL BESIDE A HIGH TRAIL.` → `EVERY STONE IS CARVED.` → `ONE MORE STONE ON THE PILE.`

segments.voice: First, what's carved. Mani stones usually carry om mani padme hum, the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion Tibetans call Chenrezig, whom you met back in year one. Some carry other mantras, a prayer, or an image of a buddha. The name comes from the mantra's second word, mani, a jewel. Second, who makes them. Skilled stone carvers, who sell or are paid for them. A family marking a death, a birth, a recovery or a hope. A pilgrim with a nail and a lot of patience. Then they're left where people pass: a pass, a bridge, a crossroads, the edge of a village, around a stupa. Over years the piles grow into long walls, built by strangers who never met. Third, the idea underneath. Tibetan teachers say a mantra carved in stone keeps sounding. A prayer flag lets the wind carry its words; a prayer wheel lets the turning hand recite; a mani stone lets the rock do it, quietly, in every weather, for as long as it lasts. That's your line: the stone chants. Not that a rock has a voice, but that the wish carved into it doesn't stop when the carver goes home. Fourth, how to pass one. Travelers keep mani walls on their right, the same clockwise respect as yesterday's kora. Stones are added, not taken: taking one home as a souvenir would be taking someone's prayer. Each new stone joins a long line of strangers' wishes for the beings who will walk this way.

segments.voice: Take a stone, a pebble, or even a scrap of paper and a pen, and slowly write one short line on it: om mani padme hum, a line from your own tradition, or one word that holds a wish for others, like kindness. Write it one letter at a time, as if carving, then hold it for a few breaths. If it's a stone, you might leave it somewhere people pass.
Mani stones. Stones carved with mantras, usually om mani padme hum, piled along paths, passes and stupas, and passed with respect on the right. Today's word.
Your line: the stone chants. One more stone on the pile, one more wish. Until tomorrow.

1315.title: Sky burial
1315.hook: in parts of Tibet the body is given to vultures: a last act of generosity, told with respect
1315.howItsDone: In parts of Tibet, after days of prayers and readings for the deceased, the body is taken at dawn to a set-apart site, where a ritual specialist prepares it and offers it to vultures while monks may chant; Tibetan teachers describe it as a final act of generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mani stones, wishes carved to keep sounding. Your line: the stone chants.

A question as old as grief: when someone we love dies, what do we do with the body? Some bury it. Some give it to fire, some to water. On the high plateau of Tibet, the ground in places is hard and stony, and wood for a fire is scarce. Over that land, wide-winged and patient, fly vultures. In parts of Tibet, families answer the question with the sky. This lesson speaks of death, gently, with respect for the families who keep this practice.
screen: `A QUESTION AS OLD AS GRIEF.` → `EARTH, FIRE, WATER.` → `IN PARTS OF TIBET, THE SKY.`

segments.voice: First, what happens, told plainly. After a death, prayers are said and texts read for the one who has died, often for several days. Then, at dawn, the body is carried to a high place set apart for this. A ritual specialist prepares it, monks or lamas may chant, and the body is offered to the vultures. Families may watch from a distance, or not at all. Tibetans call it jhator, often translated giving to the birds. Second, why the body can be given. Tibetan teachers say that by this point the mind has left. The body is like a house its owner has moved out of: still treated with care, but no longer the person. The person, in this teaching, has gone on into the in-between, the bardo you met in year one. Third, the generosity. Giving is one of the perfections a bodhisattva trains in, and Buddhist stories carry it all the way to the body. In one story of the Buddha's former lives, a young man in the forest finds a tigress so starved she is about to eat her own cubs. He has nothing else to give, so he offers himself. Sky burial, Tibetans say, carries that same spirit: a body no longer needed becomes food for living beings, so even at the very end something is given. Fourth, the respect owed. This is a family's grief and a sacred rite, not a spectacle. It leaves a listener far away a quiet question: if the body is a gift, what might we give with it while we are still using it?

1316.title: Debate
1316.hook: monks in the courtyard debate with a clap and a stamp
1316.howItsDone: In Tibetan monastic colleges, students debate daily in courtyards: a standing challenger questions a seated defender with a characteristic clap and stamp, and the defender replies from a small set of formal answers, as a way of testing and deepening understanding of the texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sky burial, a family's last gift. Your line: the last gift. Today is louder.

Crack. The sound comes over the monastery wall like a branch snapping. Then another, then laughter. Inside, in a shaded courtyard, monks in maroon robes are scattered in small groups. In each one a monk sits on the ground, calm. Another stands over him, rosary looped on his arm, and fires a question. Then he swings his right hand high, slaps it down against his left palm, and stamps his foot. The seated monk answers. Nobody here is angry. This is how they study. Today: debate.
screen: `A CRACK OVER THE WALL.` → `ONE SITS, ONE STANDS.` → `A SLAP, A STAMP, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the roles. In Tibetan monastic debate, the defender sits and holds a position. The challenger stands and tests it, asking question after question until either the position holds or the defender contradicts what he said a minute ago. Second, the clap and the stamp. Each time the challenger makes a point, he claps, right hand down onto the left palm, and stamps. It wakes everyone up. Teachers give the gesture meanings of their own; one explanation is that the clap cuts through confusion, the way a point lands. Tradition says debates open by calling on Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. Third, the rules of answering. The defender doesn't make speeches. He answers from a small set of formal replies, roughly: I accept. The reason isn't established. It doesn't follow. Every answer has to be exact, and a careless yes can be turned against him a few questions later. Students practice this for years, working through logic, the stages of the path and the nature of mind. Fourth, why a contemplative tradition shouts. Tibetan teachers say understanding that hasn't been tested is just borrowed. Debate shows whether a student actually understands emptiness or only remembers the words. And the aim is the view, not the person: monks who were slapping and stamping at each other an hour ago walk to dinner together. The goal isn't to win. It's to see clearly. In year three you met a very different debate, at Samye, where a king chose. This one happens every day, between friends.
screen: `ONE DEFENDS, ONE CHALLENGES.` · `THE CLAP AND THE STAMP.` · `I ACCEPT. NOT ESTABLISHED. DOESN'T FOLLOW.` · `TEST THE VIEW, NOT THE PERSON.` · then, large: `CLAP AND ASK.`

segments.voice: Pick something you believe without having checked it lately, about a person, about yourself, about the way things are, and say it in one plain sentence. Then stand up inside as the challenger and ask it honest questions: how do I know that? Does that always follow? You don't need to change your mind; just see where the reasoning is solid and where it's borrowed.

Your line: clap and ask. Test the view hard, and never the person. That's today, done.
